utterances.text: Mr. President, I simply note the objection to some unscheduled incidents which are contained in paragraphs -- the beginning of paragraph 39 and also paragraph 50. You've already ruled on that, in principle, and I don't have anything to add.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm wondering whether you have to repeat every time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Perhaps if it could be understood that we have a continuing objection to unscheduled incidents, I won't do that anymore.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That will be more convenient. Thank you for your understanding, Mr. Robinson. Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that will be Exhibit P1851.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: With the Court's permission, I'll read a short summary of the evidence contained in the amalgamated statement. Mr. Brennskag, a retired lieutenant-colonel from the Royal Norwegian Army, was deployed with the United Nations in Bosnia and Herzegovina on the 22nd of March, 1995, as a military observer in Sector Sarajevo. At that time, he held the rank of major. The witness was stationed in Pale until 24 May 1995. He was part of the military observer team responsible for monitoring weapons stores and weapons collection points. On the 2nd of June, 1995, the witness was posted to the side of Sector Sarajevo held by the Bosnian government. The witness confirmed that he was in Team Pofalici, based in the north of Sarajevo. A number of locations could be observed from the team's observation post. The team had a clear sight of the territory west of Sarajevo. In June 1995, it was very hectic. The witness observed up to 150 impacts incoming into Sarajevo during a 24-hour period. The witness confirms a situation report concerning an explosion in the area of Dobrinja on 18 June 1995, where the fire originated from the VRS side. Mr. Brennskag describes the use of modified air-bombs by the VRS. During his service in Sarajevo, he observed a number of modified aircraft bombs being fired from VRS positions which landed in the area of Alipasino Polje and to the east of that area. The witness investigated two incidents involving modified aircraft bombs, one on the 22nd of June, 1995, in Alipasino Polje, the other on the 1st of July, 1995. The witness also describes the shelling of the TV building and the PTT building in Sarajevo on the 28th of June, 1995. The damage to the TV building was caused by a modified aircraft bomb. He witnessed the bomb being launched from an area held by the VRS. That concludes the brief summary, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Brennskag, in paragraphs 7 to 16 of Exhibit P1851, which is your amalgamated statement now in evidence, you describe your posting in Sector Sarajevo with the Pale observer team. In paragraph 10, you state that part of your duties was to inspect two weapons collection points, one situated in Bljustavac, commonly known as Mokro barracks, and the other in Kresevo. Were these collection points the only places of inspection by the UNMO team that you were part of?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: This was the two weapon collection points, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Were those two collection points the only places where weapons were inspected by the UNMO team?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: No. There were some weapons in positions that were not in the collection points.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Whereabouts were these situated, these places?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: Those I inspected were nearby Resa [phoen] and on the other side of a canyon called Gradiste.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Who controlled the territory where the collection points were and these other areas that you have just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: This was on BSA side.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And what do you refer "BSA" to mean?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: Bosnian Serb Army.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, I call for 65 ter 23024.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Brennskag, do you recognise what is on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: Yes. This is a copy of my map which I used in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could we zoom in to the area just east of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What do -- the markings that we can see there in the area of Resa [phoen] and Gradiste, what do those markings depict?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: Those are my markings on my map where each single weapon outside the weapon collection point were situated.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you recall now what the letters and numbers signify?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry, I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: But you said that each of the markings and each of the -- if we could zoom in again further. But you're saying that each of the dots on that map signifies where a single weapon was outside the collection point?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: To what area were these weapons directed to?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: Towards the eastern part of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I seek to tender this map, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1852, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Brennskag, I wish to focus now on your posting in Sector Sarajevo on the territory held by the Bosnian Government. This is contained in paragraphs 17 to 57 of your statement. In paragraphs 17 to 18, you describe that you were posted to an observation team called "Team Pofalici," which had its observation post in a hill north of the city. Where, exactly, was the OP located?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: This OP was located on the hills, on the place called Vitkovac.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, can I have 65 ter 23025.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you recognise what is shown on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: Yes. It's a map of a part of Sarajevo. And in 2006, I marked the OP, the observation post, with the triangle you can see on the map.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: That triangle is in blue, just above the word "Vitkovac"; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I seek to tender that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1853, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: In paragraph 36 of your statement, you said that you saw the first modified air-bomb, during your time as an observer in the Pofalici team, around the middle of June 1995. From what location did you observe this from?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: It could be from the OP, and it could be also from other places where I were working in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: How many modified air-bombs did you observe during your time as an UNMO?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: Around four or five, six.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What direction did the modified air-bombs come from?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: Apart from the bomb I investigated at the 2nd of June -- of July, mostly, as I remember, from the west.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you know the name of the area where the -- that you're referring to as being west?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: Yes. It's the area which we called "Ilidza area."

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Who controlled this position at that time?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: At that time, it was a BSA area.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: How did you know that they were modified air-bombs?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: I didn't at first know that it was modified air-bombs. But as I got to know and when I was observing, and when I was investigating the impacts, I learned now that this was modified air-bombs.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Was there any -- anything that you could notice as this projectile was in the air?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: Yes. They had, in a part of their flight, a smoke tail from a rocket.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You also said that you got to know that they were air-bombs when you were investigating the impacts. How were you able to determine that they were, in fact, modified air-bombs?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: You saw the rest of the rocket when we investigated the impact.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And, in particular, what do you mean when you -- can you describe what you mean by "the rest of the rocket"?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: It was mounted on the shrapnel or the rest of the bomb.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And how was that different to the other sorts of shells?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: Artillery or mortar don't have any rocket rests on their -- that you can find when it has exploded.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: In paragraph 52 of your statement, you describe witnessing the TV building in Sarajevo being hit by a modified air-bomb. Where were you at the time that you witnessed this event?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: This morning, I was on my job at the observation post at Vitkovac.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What direction did the modified air-bomb come from?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: The direction of the -- where it come from, from Ilidza area.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And, again, at this time on the 28th of June, 1995, who was controlling this position at Ilidza?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: It was still BSA.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. That concludes my examination. I seek to tender into evidence the associated exhibits listed in Appendix A and Confidential Appendix B to the Rule 92 ter notification. And I have a correction to make to the Rule 92 ter filing, and I apologise for this. It was -- there's a typographical error in paragraph 2 of the notification in a sentence. A change was made in paragraph 48 by the deletion of a reference number, 65 ter 14919, in fact, should read "14939." And that is also in paragraph 3(b). In relation to Confidential -- sorry, in relation to Appendix A; the first associated exhibit has the 65 ter number 10002, and that's the witness's statement from May 1996. I don't seek to tender the statement, but I wish to tender the three -- in the comments column, it says "Two maps attached," but, in fact, there's two maps and a diagram. The first map, ERN -- sorry, the first diagram, ERN 0039-1399 is referred to in paragraph 54 of the witness's statement, and that -- Mr. Reid has given these three documents new 65 ter numbers so that they are single exhibits and not attached to the witness statement, because we don't want the witness statement into evidence. So that 65 ter number is 23026. Then there is a map with an ERN number 0039-1400 that's referred to in paragraph 49 of the amalgamated statement. That is 65 ter 23023. The second map, which is the one that we just looked at, that is now Exhibit P15 -- 1852. The second 65 ter number is -- in the column is 10143, and again that's the witness's October 2006 statement. I don't seek to tender the statement, but I wish to tender the map which is attached. And this was an oversight in not listing that in the comments column. The map has an ERN of 0604-9663. It's referred to in paragraph 18 of the witness's statement, and the 65 ter number is 23025.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Which we have admitted now a minute ago. We admitted --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, yes, and that is --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: 1853, yes, you're correct. Then the next in line is the transcripts of the witness's evidence in Milosevic and Perisic. We don't seek to tender. Neither do we seek to tender associated Exhibit 14731. But we do seek to tender the remaining exhibits listed there. One already has been admitted. That is P1528.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Why --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: In relation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why under seal, the last item?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Simply, as I've explained with previous witnesses, where it's been an under-seal exhibit in another case, I've put it in the confidential appendix for this purpose, but that exhibit can be tendered publicly in this trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any objection, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. With respect to that last document, 09814, the amalgamated -- first of all, it's a 33-page police report about this incident, and the amalgamated statement simply says that this document confirms the witness's presence at the scene of that incident. We don't think that that's a sufficient basis to admit the entire report.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I -- at this stage, I would ask that two pages of that exhibit be -- if two pages, 0090-5111 to 0090-5112, could be admitted from that exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let me take a brief look at para 48. I take it there's no opposition in that case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll admit them all. To make clear -- again, to make it clear: His personal note is not being tendered?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Brennskag.

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Before I begin, I would like to express my gratitude for meeting with the Defence team, and I hope that the cross-examination will go smoothly because of that. Are you able to tell me, with these three observation points at the Muslim side, how many observation points did you have on the Serbian side in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: I'm not sure what you mean. I was working on one observation post inside Sarajevo. At my time on the Bosnian Serb side, I had no fixed observation post.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I were to tell you that, on the Serbian side, you always had from 11 to 13 observation posts, or four to five times more than in the Muslim side, would that correspond to what you know about this?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: I am not able to remember how many observation posts Sector Sarajevo had.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that the UN Military Observer teams, and their staff in their headquarters in Sarajevo, received reports and reported back every day orally and in writing? Mr. Brennskag, did you receive a translation?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: Oh, yes. I'm just reading it. Normally, our UN observer military HQ in Sarajevo got -- received reports every day from their teams.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. May I ask you, what was your mandate, exactly? What was it that you were observing and what were you reporting on?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: As military observer, my mandate was to inspect weapon collection points, or let me say that the Total Exclusion Zone of 20 K around Sarajevo was in order, and the next mandate for the observer team was the anti-sniper deal inside Sarajevo. Then we also had a mandate to investigate impacts of heavy weapon on both side of the confrontation line.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. If I could just make a suggestion, and I realise the witness is not speaking in his native language, but I think he's distracted by the monitor when he's giving his answers. And it might be easier for him if he gives the answer without following the reading, because he seems to be doing that, and it's making the -- making the testimony somehow not very smooth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Without having the benefit of interpretation, I can understand that. But do we have difficulty in following him?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Not difficulty in following him, but the evidence is very slow, and it may affect the time that Dr. Karadzic has for his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll bear that in mind, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And did you conduct these investigations that you mentioned in your previous answer?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: I conducted investigations of impacts at my time as an observer inside Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What was the objective of those investigations? What did they encompass?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: My job was to investigate the impacts that was told me from my UNMO HQ in Sarajevo, and the objective of those investigations is my -- I can't understand, sorry. The objectives of those investigations is the UNMO HQ to tell.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And was the objective to establish the type of weapons, or the projectiles, and elements which would, without doubt, prove which side had fired the shot?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: When we investigated an impact, it was always to find what kind of weapon was fired, the direction from where the firing were coming, and, in case it was possible, to find the point of firing. And, of course, if we were able to do it, it was to find what happened around the impact; injuries or so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And were these investigations, in the criminal legal sense, investigations which would establish without doubt the perpetrators and the consequences?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: We delivered our investigation report as a part of a whole investigation of an impact, and it was the UNMO HQ and UNPROFOR to decide exactly what was happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So you established the direction from which a projectile came. Did you also establish the distance from which it came, or did you try to calculate the position -- the location from where the projectile was fired? To be more precise: In how many cases was it possible to determine the distance?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: At your last question, I don't remember. At your first question, it was not always possible to find from -- the firing point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you make some sort of selection about the events that you were reporting on or did you report everything that was happening?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: When I was on the observation post, we reported what we were able to detect as impacts, and we always had to be two observers to agree, what we saw or heard, before we reported it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And how unimportant did an event have to be that it would not be included in your report?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: I have to answer that I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I may help you. Can we consider it that what you reported on was important and what you did not report on was not important?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: Everything we reported were, for us, important.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But what you didn't report on you considered unimportant; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: No, it's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So there were some important things that you didn't report about; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: I can confirm that there were some evidence we didn't report, but they were not -- that was not why, they were not important.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What were the reasons, then?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: At times, it was very, very busy, and two observers were not able to report everything that happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you just briefly tell us: What were the restrictions or limitations you had in your work? Now I'm speaking about your work in Sarajevo, in the Muslim part of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: Normally, we should have freedom of movement as observers. This is not -- this was not true. Inside Sarajevo, the ABiH put restrictions on our movements; where to go, when to go there, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did that prevent you from getting an insight into certain events of which you wanted to report?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: Yes, of course, because we were not allowed to go close to the confrontation line, as they said to us, for our own safety.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it true that you heard that among the UN troops, there had been rumours about Muslims shooting at their own civilians?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: It may happen that I heard those rumours, but I can't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree with me that you saw the BiH Army opening fire from Sarajevo? Most usually, the fire was mortar fire; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: I saw and heard BiH Army firing mortars from BiH side, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you were on that side, you couldn't see where the shells fell in the Serbian part of Sarajevo? It was not customary for monitors from one side to cross over to the other side; right?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: From my --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sorry. Compound question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: There are two questions. Can you answer the question, Mr. Brennskag?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I answered the question: From my side inside Sarajevo, I could not see the impacts of those mortars firing from inside Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And the second question was this: Was it customary for monitors to cross from one side to the other side across the confrontation line or did they actually stick to their original side?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: I entered Sarajevo -- inside Sarajevo, on the BiH side, at the 2nd of June, and at that time, sector UN observers -- Sector Sarajevo did not have any observers on BSA side, and we, inside Sarajevo, were not allowed to go across the line and inspect on BSA side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What were your observation posts known as? What were they called?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: I can only remember exactly my own observation post, and this was on the hills of Vitkovac. And as far as I remember, it was called Sierra Victor 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it also correct that you observed that the Muslim side had opened mobile mortar fire, and after that, the mobile mortars were moved to a different position?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: I didn't observe that the firing from mortars were mobile, but we knew that they -- after the firing, they moved the weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree with me that you were aware -- that you had either seen, yourself, or learned from others that the Muslim forces deployed their mortars close to your positions; for example, close to the PTT building and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: We knew that the BiH -- ABiH had mortars in a junkyard downhill from our OP, but I was never able to spot the mortars visually.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you establish that the Bosnian Army, as you call it, set up its military positions in the civilian zones, which, according to you, they should not have done?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: I'm not sure of the word you mean, "establish."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you see them do that? Were you sure that they were doing something that they were not supposed to do, that they should not have done?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: I did not see any weapon positions, as I earlier said, inside Sarajevo. We knew they had weapons; for example, what I said about the mortars in the junkyard. And, also, if they had weapon positions close or inside civilian area, where civilian people are living, they shouldn't do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Allow me to quote a sentence from your statement provided on the 26th of October, 2006. On page 4: [In English] "I did see the Bosnians establish military position within civilian areas, which is something they should not have done." [Interpretation] Is this your sentence, a sentence from your statement?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: Yes. I said first that I didn't see any weapon positions. I know -- and I visited military offices inside Sarajevo, close to where people were living.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You also stated that, judging by the fire, you could establish that the fire had been opened from 80-millimetre mortars, and those were the mortars that were deployed within the city of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: I know that they were firing from that junkyard, as I have stated before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You also stated, did you not, in the Dragomir Milosevic case, on the 8th of March, 2007, on page 3492: [In English] "Several times I saw soldiers in the uniform of the BH-held side of Sarajevo"?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: Yes, there were a lot of soldiers in uniform, or uniformed people, inside Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You also saw, close to your observation post, a 55 tank belonging to the BiH Army; right?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: Yes, I saw this every time I went to my OP on Vitkovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You also realise that Alipasino Polje and the "Oslobodjenje" building were close to the PTT building, and that trenches and a front-line were in front of the two of them; right?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: No, I didn't see any trenches in the place where I call Alipasino Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you know where the "Oslobodjenje" building was? And if you do, could you tell us whether that building was on the front-line, itself?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: I can't remember where the "Oslobodjenje" building was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that the 1st Corps of the BiH Army was deployed in the Muslim part of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If you didn't know the name of that strategic unit, did you at least know the names -- the deployment of brigades in Sarajevo? I'm talking about Muslim brigades in the Muslim part of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: I can't remember the deployment of the brigades inside Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could the Court please produce 65 ter document 14731. I would like to jog your memory of the things that you once noted. Can this be blown up. I don't think that there is a translation. Or, rather, there is. Can we have the English and the Norwegian page. We don't need the translation in Serbian. Instead of Serbian, if available, can we see the Norwegian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are these your notes, sir?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: Yes, it's my personal notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the third paragraph after the date, it says: [In English] "All that I have left from that time is a loose collection of personal notes." [Interpretation] Can you tell us where these notes are, and would it be possible to use them?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: These notes were made for me, I think, around 2001, and they were at that time meant just for me. Some of the comments are what I had observed and seen, some of the comments are just my own thoughts, and some of the comments are second-hand information collected after the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You stated at one point that the two of us had never met; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree with me that now I have the right to be shocked, when I read the fifth paragraph in your notes, where it says: "I also write this article with a sense of shock that neither Radovan Karadzic nor Ratko Mladic have been arrested ..." And so on and so on. [Interpretation] Why were you in a state of shock, given the fact that the two of us do not have any sort of history together?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: As I said, this is my personal notes, and it was meant for me. And you have the right to react as you want.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is your shock now over, and can I take it that your testimony here today has been and will continue to be impartial?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: I don't know any answer to that question. Could you please be more correct?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now go to page 16. I am still confident that your state of shock that you once felt will pass in the course of this testimony. It's the previous page in English -- or, rather, in Norwegian. The section that I'm interested in is on the previous page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can I draw your attention to the last paragraph in English, and I believe that you will find the case to be the same in Norwegian. You were talking about military units within Sarajevo in the summer of 1995.

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And then you say that BiH liaison officers at the headquarters for UN Sector Sarajevo were Captain Edvo and Captain Nermin, and then you say that the Command of the 1st Corps was close to the October Square; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: Yes. It's the office, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does it arise from all that that you knew that the 1st Corps consisted of the 12th Division, the 14th Division, and the 16th Division, and that the 12th Division was deployed in the city of Sarajevo, itself?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: I can't say the accuracy of this note. This was my personal notes, what I had managed to obtain. And what is correct of it, I can't say today.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well, but these are your notes. You either checked all that or you believed somebody's words. Do you know that the 12th Division consisted of brigades and that they were deployed in the Muslim part of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: It's two questions. I try to ask -- to answer the first question, if I had checked all that or you believed somebody's words. I noted this, what I heard, for myself. As to the second question, do you know that the 12th Division consisted of brigades and that they were deployed in the Muslim part of Sarajevo, I didn't exactly know.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we go to the following pages, both in English and Norwegian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: To console you, sir, I can tell you that your notes are absolutely correct. Does it say here that the Staff of the 111th Brigade was in the city and that the Staff of the 112th Brigade was close to the Dolac Railway Station, and then the 115th Brigade had its headquarters in Stari Grad, and the 152nd Brigade headquarters was in the old part of the town of Kovaci, and then the 155th Brigade had its headquarters at Dobrinja? Is all that correct?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: I said I'm not sure if my notes are correct. But if you say it's correct, maybe I have got my notes correct. But this was what I heard in meetings or from others. I did not exactly check where those positions -- where they were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was going to rise a moment ago to say: Can the accused be told to refrain from making comments and put questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's move on, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you see that the Slavne Olovska Brigade was headquartered near Buco Potok and that Buco Potok was very close to Vitkovac, where your OP was?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: I don't know where this position is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. When we look at the map, then we will establish it. Does it not say here that the Tvrtko Brigade had its headquarters in Cengic Vila, and the Staff of the 1st Mechanised Brigade was near Hrasno, and of the 102nd Mechanised Brigade, its headquarters was close to Dolac, and outside of Sarajevo, at Igman, was the 82nd Mountain Brigade, in Hrasnicki Stan, Hrasnica, 181st Brigade, and in Hrasnica itself the 104th Brigade; is that correct? Did you not write that in your notes about the deployment in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: I don't have a map here. I noted what's stated in my personal notes, but I don't know where the positions are.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we -- can I just read just one sentence of Article 31 of your statement: [In English] "It was a very hectic time. There could be up to 150 impacts incoming into Sarajevo during a 24-hour period."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that in June, a large Muslim offensive began to unblock Sarajevo, as they called it?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we look at page 10, and that will be the last thing for today. Page 10 of this same document, please. Page 10 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll adjourn for today. We'll continue next week. I was told that --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- we need to adjourn right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I misunderstood the situation. It is my understanding that you have to leave by 4.30 on Monday.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've already told that I had to leave Monday, not the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think that's arranged by the -- is there any reason why we should not sit in the morning on Monday, then?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, there is a reason for that for Monday. We are supposed to have a videolink testimony, which should be conducted in the afternoon, because the morning session should be used by another Chamber which uses the same videolink. I think you will have about less than two hours on Monday, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It was suggested to us by the Court Deputy to sit in the morning, to conclude the evidence of this witness in the morning, and then we continue with videolink in the afternoon, if that is agreeable to the parties.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I say what I think. May I say what I think. Namely, Mr. Brennskag speaks Norwegian. He doesn't speak Serbian or English. On the other hand, the Prosecution has no restrictions in relation to written materials that they can introduce through this witness. So I believe that the time that -- that the time allocated to me, in view of the mother tongue of Mr. Brennskag and the slow manner in which he's responding, is overly restrictive, and I would kindly like to have this matter reviewed once more. I understood that Mr. Brennskag did not have to leave, but that somebody else told him that he had to leave on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It is the VWS that arranged the travel arrangement for him. And I don't agree with your observation that he does not speak English. His English is just perfect. I don't see any problem.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With all due respect, Brennskag, himself -- Mr. Brennskag, himself, has said that he needs to read it. I understand that he understands English, but he also needs to read it, and this is taking up a lot of our time. So if it may be permitted, that I can remind Mr. Brennskag of what we have here. BH starts an offensive -- [In English] "The offensive gradually peters up to the BS intensifies its bombardment of Sarajevo and other so-called safe areas." [Interpretation] Therefore, you were aware of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, we'll --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- the offensive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll continue on Monday.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I was just going to say that Your Honour had already decided that we would not continue further for today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we will adjourn today, but there are a couple of other matters. If it is agreeable to the parties and staff, we will resume on Monday at 9.00, and the conclusion of which we'll resume to hear the next witness through videolink at 2.15. Monday may be a long day for all of us. And in relation to - is it the 26th motion? I didn't count - which requested for an adjournment or suspension, we've received the response from the Prosecution. Whatever the decision we may make, it is our opinion that immediate [indiscernible] is not warranted, so we'll continue next week, and we'll try to issue our decision as soon as possible. Mr. Brennskag, we'll adjourn for today and resume tomorrow morning -- yes, Monday morning, and please be reminded that you are not supposed to discuss your testimony with anybody else. Please have a nice weekend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 1st day of November, 2010, at 9.00 a.m.
